Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad).
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] MSSQL sqlservr.exe spawning OS shell via xp_cmdshell (XEntry Team) · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Scheduled task created with suspicious image / encoded args · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Unsanctioned RMM trio deployment: Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → [LLM] Server-side BitLocker mass encryption enablement (XEntry Team extortion) · [LLM] BitLocker recovery key harvesting via manage-bde -protectors -get · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
MSSQL sqlservr.exe spawning OS shell via xp_cmdshell (XEntry Team) AIExploitation High
Hunts the XEntry Team's initial execution vector: a misconfigured internet-exposed Microsoft SQL Server 2019 running commands through the xp_cmdshell extended stored procedure, which manifests as sqlservr.exe directly spawning cmd.exe/powershell.exe child processes. This is the pivot the actor used to move from DBMS access to full OS-level command execution. Rationale: Anchored on the article's explicit statement that Microsoft SQL Server 2019 was misconfigured to allow OS command execution via xp_cmdshell; sqlservr.exe spawning a shell is a high-fidelity, rarely-legitimate parent/child pair. Cross-checked against Huntress MSSQL xp_cmdshell attack writeups. Cross-checked against: • https://www.huntress.com/blog/attacking-mssql-servers-pt-ii • https://securelist.com/new-extortion-scheme-printers-bitlocker/120718/
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1505.001 T1190
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • DBA-approved xp_cmdshell jobs running maintenance batch scripts
  • SQL Agent jobs shelling out to robocopy/backup utilities
  • Monitoring agents that query OS metrics via xp_cmdshell
  • Legit ETL packages invoking cmd for file moves
Suppression filter
| where not (ProcessCommandLine has_any ("\\backup\\","robocopy","xp_cmdshell 'bcp") and InitiatingProcessAccountName endswith "$")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine of the child and the SQL instance account context; determine if xp_cmdshell is intentionally enabled and whether this instance is internet-exposed on 1433. 2) Contain: disable xp_cmdshell (sp_configure), block inbound 1433 from internet ranges at the firewall, and rotate the SQL service/SA credentials — check GitHub for leaked connection strings. 3) Hunt: review subsequent processes on the host for RMM installs (Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM), web shell writes to IIS/wwwroot, and any manage-bde activity.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "sqlservr.exe"
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","reg.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where tolower(ParentProcessName) endswith "sqlservr.exe"
| where NewProcessName has_any ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","net.exe","net1.exe","whoami.exe","reg.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Server-side BitLocker mass encryption enablement (XEntry Team extortion) AIActions on Objectives High
Hunts the XEntry Team / RDP-BitLocker actor's impact stage: enabling BitLocker on servers and data drives via manage-bde -on or Enable-BitLocker with a numerical recovery password, deployed through RMM/scheduled tasks/GPO to encrypt disks and hold recovery keys for ransom. Targets encryption being turned ON on hosts (especially servers) where it is not part of normal provisioning. Rationale: Directly maps the article's core impact: 'enabling the BitLocker service and individually encrypting the infrastructure's disks, generating a key for each encrypted system.' manage-bde -on and Enable-BitLocker -RecoveryPassword are the exact commands that turn on encryption and generate a per-host recovery key. Corroborated by BlackHills/NCC BitLocker-ransomware research and Splunk Security Content. Cross-checked against: • https://www.blackhillsinfosec.com/bitlocker-ransomware-using-bitlocker-for-nefarious-reasons/ • https://research.splunk.com/endpoint/d0e6ec70-6e40-41a2-8b93-8d9ff077a746/
ATT&CKT1486 T1490 T1657
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • IT provisioning newly-imaged laptops with BitLocker via MDT/SCCM
  • Compliance-driven bulk BitLocker rollout on endpoints
  • Intune/GPO-managed BitLocker enablement on corporate fleet
  • Admin re-enabling BitLocker after a hardware/firmware change
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe","tsmanager.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("ccmexec.exe","intunemanagementextension.exe"))
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm whether the host is a server/data store (unusual BitLocker target) and whether the enablement originated from an RMM agent, scheduled task, or GPO rather than your MDM baseline; capture the recovery key ID from the cmdline. 2) Contain: isolate the host, suspend the scheduled task/GPO driving the encryption domain-wide, and escrow/retrieve the recovery password from AD (msFVE-RecoveryInformation) before the attacker removes protectors. 3) Hunt: correlate for simultaneous manage-bde runs across many hosts, GPO changes on the DC, and RMM installs in the preceding days; look for 'Hacked by XEntry Team' strings and print-spooler ransom jobs.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where (FileName =~ "manage-bde.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-on")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Enable-BitLocker","-RecoveryPassword","-RecoveryPasswordProtector"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "manage-bde.exe" and CommandLine has "-on")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Enable-BitLocker","-RecoveryPassword"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: BitLocker Encryption Enabled via manage-bde or Enable-BitLocker
id: b3d92a4f-1e77-4a5c-8f21-0c6b9e4d1a55
description: Detects BitLocker being switched ON via manage-bde -on or the Enable-BitLocker PowerShell cmdlet with a recovery password, an extortion technique used by the XEntry Team to encrypt server disks.
references:

source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 ((@Image:(*\manage-bde.exe OR *\Manage-bde.exe OR *\MANAGE-BDE.EXE) AND @CommandLine:*-on*) OR (@Image:(*\powershell.exe OR *\PowerShell.exe) AND @CommandLine:(*Enable-BitLocker* OR *-RecoveryPassword*)))

| (ImageFileName=/\\manage-bde\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/-on/i) OR (ImageFileName=/\\(powershell|pwsh)\.exe$/i AND CommandLine=/(Enable-BitLocker|-RecoveryPassword)/i)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name="manage-bde.exe" AND Processes.process="*-on*") OR (Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") AND Processes.process="*Enable-BitLocker*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | convert ctime(firstTime) ctime(lastTime)
Unsanctioned RMM trio deployment: Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM AICommand & Control Medium
Hunts the XEntry Team's C2/persistence layer: stacking multiple legitimate RMM tools (ManageEngine Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM) on victim hosts as a resilient control channel. The behavioural signal is the co-occurrence of MULTIPLE distinct RMM agent families on the same host or estate, which is abnormal for sanctioned IT. Rationale: The article names all three RMM families (ManageEngine Endpoint Central, Mesh Agent, Tactical RMM) deployed together for persistence/C2. Requiring >=2 distinct families on one host suppresses the noise of a single sanctioned RMM while catching the attacker's tool-stacking pattern. Kaspersky's report notes >20% of incidents abuse RMM for C2. Cross-checked against: • https://securelist.com/new-extortion-scheme-printers-bitlocker/120718/
ATT&CKT1219 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • MSP migration period where old and new RMM agents co-exist
  • IT trialing a replacement RMM before decommissioning the incumbent
  • Vendor support session installing a temporary Mesh/Tactical agent
  • Endpoint Central deployed alongside a separate patch-management RMM by design
Response runbook
1) Triage: verify each RMM family against your sanctioned-tooling inventory; identify the installer's parent process and the account/host that pushed it (RMM installed by sqlservr.exe or a scheduled task is highly suspect). 2) Contain: block the RMM cloud endpoints at the proxy, kill/uninstall the unauthorized agents, and disable the deploying scheduled task/GPO. 3) Hunt: pivot on the install account across the domain for lateral spread, check for BitLocker enablement and DC GPO modifications, and review outbound beaconing to Mesh/Tactical/Endpoint Central relay domains.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where FileName in~ ("meshagent.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","tacticalagent.exe","dcagentservice.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","uems.exe","desktopcentral.exe")
| extend Family = case(FileName has "mesh","MeshAgent", FileName has "tactical","TacticalRMM", "EndpointCentral")
| summarize Families = make_set(Family), Binaries = make_set(FileName), FirstSeen = min(Timestamp) by DeviceName
| where array_length(Families) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has_any ("meshagent.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","tacticalagent.exe","dcagentservice.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","UEMS.exe","DesktopCentral.exe")
| extend Family = case(NewProcessName has "mesh","MeshAgent", NewProcessName has "tactical","TacticalRMM", "EndpointCentral")
| summarize Families = make_set(Family), Binaries = make_set(NewProcessName), FirstSeen = min(TimeGenerated) by Computer
| where array_length(Families) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\meshagent.exe OR *\MeshAgent.exe OR *\tacticalrmm.exe OR *\tacticalagent.exe OR *\dcagentservice.exe OR *\dcagenttrayicon.exe OR *\UEMS.exe OR *\DesktopCentral.exe)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(meshagent|tacticalrmm|tacticalagent|dcagentservice|dcagenttrayicon|UEMS|DesktopCentral)\.exe$/i
| case { ImageFileName=/mesh/i | family:="MeshAgent" ; ImageFileName=/tactical/i | family:="TacticalRMM" ; * | family:="EndpointCentral" }
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName], function=collect([family]))
| length(family) >= 2
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count values(Processes.process_name) as processes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("meshagent.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","tacticalagent.exe","dcagentservice.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","UEMS.exe","DesktopCentral.exe") by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval mesh=if(match(processes,"meshagent"),1,0), tactical=if(match(processes,"tactical"),1,0), endpointcentral=if(match(processes,"dcagent|UEMS|DesktopCentral"),1,0) | eval rmm_families=mesh+tactical+endpointcentral | where rmm_families>=2
| tstats summariesonly=false count values(Processes.process_name) as processes from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name IN ("meshagent.exe","tacticalrmm.exe","tacticalagent.exe","dcagentservice.exe","dcagenttrayicon.exe","UEMS.exe","DesktopCentral.exe") by Processes.dest | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | eval mesh=if(match(processes,"meshagent"),1,0), tactical=if(match(processes,"tactical"),1,0), endpointcentral=if(match(processes,"dcagent|UEMS|DesktopCentral"),1,0) | eval rmm_families=mesh+tactical+endpointcentral | where rmm_families>=2
BitLocker recovery key harvesting via manage-bde -protectors -get AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts the collection step where the XEntry Team used RMM tooling to enumerate and exfiltrate per-host BitLocker recovery keys before/after encryption, via manage-bde -protectors -get or (Get-BitLockerVolume).KeyProtector. Distinct pivot from the encryption-enable UC: this catches key extraction, which is how the actor retains the ransom leverage. Rationale: Maps the article's caption 'Commands executed through RMM tools to collect BitLocker keys.' manage-bde -protectors -get and Get-BitLockerVolume KeyProtector are the canonical ways to read the recovery password, and reading keys at scale (especially from an RMM parent) is rare in benign ops. Corroborated by BlackHills BitLocker-ransomware detection guidance. Cross-checked against: • https://www.blackhillsinfosec.com/bitlocker-ransomware-using-bitlocker-for-nefarious-reasons/ • https://securelist.com/new-extortion-scheme-printers-bitlocker/120718/
ATT&CKT1005 T1552.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Helpdesk retrieving a recovery key for a locked-out user
  • MDM/Intune escrow validation scripts reading KeyProtector
  • Sysadmin auditing BitLocker protector status during compliance checks
  • Backup software querying BitLocker volume state
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("intunemanagementextension.exe","ccmexec.exe") or AccountName endswith "-helpdesk")
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the parent process and account — key enumeration launched from an RMM agent, sqlservr.exe, or a scheduled task on multiple hosts is the attacker pattern, whereas a single helpdesk invocation is benign. 2) Contain: if unsanctioned, isolate affected hosts, force-rotate BitLocker keys and re-escrow to AD/Azure, and revoke the executing account. 3) Hunt: correlate with manage-bde -on enablement events, RMM installs, and any staging/exfil of the collected keys to attacker infrastructure; expand across all domain-synced systems.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(14d)
| where (FileName =~ "manage-bde.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "-protectors" and ProcessCommandLine has "-get")
    or (FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and ProcessCommandLine has_any ("Get-BitLockerVolume","KeyProtector","RecoveryPassword"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessParentFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(14d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where (NewProcessName endswith "manage-bde.exe" and CommandLine has "-protectors" and CommandLine has "-get")
    or (NewProcessName has_any ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe") and CommandLine has_any ("Get-BitLockerVolume","KeyProtector","RecoveryPassword"))
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc

SecurityEvent

Iran War Cyber Threat Landscape | A Midyear Assessment on What Matters

SentinelLabs
2026-07-21 8 use cases 2 techniques 6 kill-chain phases detected

In April, SentinelLABS’ Tom Hegel published an initial assessment of the first five weeks of the conflict. Three months later, the evidence supports refinement.

ATT&CKT1190 T1566
Click any ATT&CK pill below to open it on the Matrix

Delivery
Detected

Exploitation

Detected

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Masqueraded uxtheme.dll dropped outside Windows dirs via SysAid/RMM deployment (Cavern Manticore) · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] AppDomainManager hijacking config artifact dropped in user-writable path (Screening Serpens/UNC1549) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Cavern Manticore WinDirStat DLL side-load of fake uxtheme.dll (Cavern backdoor) · RMM tool installed by non-IT user — remote-access utility for hands-on-keyboard
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage.
Cavern Manticore WinDirStat DLL side-load of fake uxtheme.dll (Cavern backdoor) AIInstallation High
Hunts the specific defense-evasion step where a legitimate signed WinDirStat binary loads an attacker-supplied uxtheme.dll (the Cavern modular C2 backdoor) from its own directory instead of System32. This is the exact side-load Check Point documented for the Iran-nexus Cavern Manticore actor deployed via abused SysAid/RMM access. Rationale: windirstat.exe + a co-located uxtheme.dll outside Windows system dirs is the exact side-load Check Point named for Cavern Manticore; uxtheme.dll almost never loads from a non-Windows path legitimately, making this near-zero FP. Cross-checked Check Point Research and cybersecuritynews write-ups. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable/extracted WinDirStat build run from a Downloads or Temp folder that ships its own theming redistributable
  • Malware-analysis sandbox that stages system DLLs alongside sample binaries
  • Developer copying a Windows uxtheme.dll next to a test build for debugging
  • Application-virtualization (App-V/MSIX) layers presenting DLLs from a virtual path
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFolderPath !startswith @"C:\Program Files"
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the DllSHA256 and HostSHA256 from the hit; confirm windirstat.exe is the genuine signed binary and the uxtheme.dll is unsigned/unknown — a mismatch confirms side-load. 2) Contain: isolate the host, capture the folder containing both files, and block the DLL hash across the fleet. 3) Hunt: check how the bundle arrived — look for SysAid/RMM agent processes writing these files, and pivot on the host's outbound connections for Cavern modular C2 beacons.
DeviceImageLoadEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName =~ "windirstat.exe"
| where FileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\System32" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, HostProcess=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, HostSHA256=InitiatingProcessSHA256, LoadedDllPath=FolderPath, DllSHA256=SHA256, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
Event
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where Source == "Microsoft-Windows-Sysmon" and EventID == 7
| where EventData has "windirstat.exe" and EventData has "uxtheme.dll"
| where EventData !has @"C:\Windows\System32" and EventData !has @"C:\Windows\SysWOW64" and EventData !has @"C:\Windows\WinSxS"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, EventID, RenderedDescription
title: Cavern Manticore WinDirStat Side-Load of Fake uxtheme.dll
id: 6c2f1a94-7d3e-4a1b-9f2c-3b8e5d0a71c4
description: Detects legitimate windirstat.exe loading uxtheme.dll from outside Windows system directories, the Cavern Manticore backdoor side-load.
references:
  - https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/
  - https://www.sentinelone.com/labs/iran-war-cyber-threat-landscape-a-midyear-assessment-on-what-matters/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1574.002
  - attack.t1036.005
logsource:
  category: image_load
  product: windows
detection:
  selection:
    Image|endswith: '\windirstat.exe'
    ImageLoaded|endswith: '\uxtheme.dll'
  filter_sys:
    ImageLoaded|startswith:
      - 'C:\Windows\System32'
      - 'C:\Windows\SysWOW64'
      - 'C:\Windows\WinSxS'
  condition: selection and not filter_sys
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where Processes.process_name="windirstat.exe" NOT (Processes.process_path IN ("*\\Program Files\\*","*\\Program Files (x86)\\*")) by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.process_name Processes.process_path Processes.process Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)`

Masqueraded uxtheme.dll dropped outside Windows dirs via SysAid/RMM deployment (Cavern Manticore) AIDelivery High
Hunts the delivery/lateral-movement step where Cavern Manticore abuses an existing SysAid software-deployment feature (or other RMM agent) to write the WinDirStat bundle — a fake uxtheme.dll masquerading as a system DLL — onto a target machine. Surfaces the writing (parent) process so the abused RMM/deployment tool is identified without hardcoding its name. Rationale: uxtheme.dll is a core Windows DLL that legitimately exists only under C:\Windows; any write elsewhere is the Cavern Manticore masqueraded backdoor. Surfacing the WriterProcess/WriterParent identifies the abused SysAid/RMM deployment tool (article's key point: no SysAid CVE, legitimate feature abused). Cross-checked Check Point and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2026/cavern-manticore-exposing-iran-linked-modular-c2-framework/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/cavern-manticore-abuses-sysaid-rmm-and-windirstat-dll-sideloading/
ATT&CKT1072 T1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Portable WinDirStat distribution unzipped to a user folder that bundles a themed DLL
  • Software packaging/repackaging tools staging system DLLs into a build directory under ProgramData
  • Backup or migration tooling restoring a full profile tree that includes a copied uxtheme.dll
  • Endpoint DLL-redirection/app-compat shim tooling copying system DLLs beside an app
Suppression filter
| where WriterProcess !in~ ("msiexec.exe","7z.exe","winrar.exe","explorer.exe") or InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("sysaid","rmm","deploy")
Response runbook
1) Triage: hash the dropped uxtheme.dll and inspect WriterProcess/WriterParent — if the writer is a SysAid/RMM agent or an unexpected service account, treat as active deployment-tool abuse. 2) Contain: isolate the destination host, suspend the RMM deployment job/account, and revoke the RMM agent's credentials pending review. 3) Hunt: enumerate every host that received the same job from that RMM console, and hunt for windirstat.exe loading the DLL plus Cavern modular C2 egress.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where FolderPath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, DroppedDllPath=FolderPath, SHA256, WriterProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, WriterPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, WriterCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine, WriterParent=InitiatingProcessParentFileName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName =~ "uxtheme.dll"
| where TargetFilePath !startswith @"C:\Windows\"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

AppDomainManager hijacking config artifact dropped in user-writable path (Screening Serpens/UNC1549) AIExploitation Medium
Hunts the .NET AppDomainManager hijack Unit 42 flagged as Screening Serpens' key 2026 evolution: an application .exe.config is planted in a user-writable directory (Downloads/Temp/AppData/ProgramData/Public) to force a signed .NET host to load a malicious managed assembly (MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2) before EDR inspects it. Config drops of this kind in those paths are rare outside developer tooling. Rationale: AppDomainManager hijacking (the technique Unit 42 named as Screening Serpens' critical 2026 evolution) requires a planted .exe.config redirecting a signed .NET host to a malicious assembly; a .exe.config appearing in Downloads/Temp/AppData outside dev tooling is the detectable artifact. Content isn't in file telemetry, so this is scoped as hunting. Cross-checked Unit 42 and cybersecuritynews. Cross-checked against: • https://unit42.paloaltonetworks.com/tracking-iran-apt-screening-serpens/ • https://cybersecuritynews.com/iranian-hackers-abuse-appdomainmanager-hijacking/
ATT&CKT1574.014 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer building/running .NET apps from a Downloads or repo folder under AppData
  • ClickOnce or portable .NET apps that ship their own app.config beside the exe in ProgramData
  • CI/build agents or unit-test runners emitting *.exe.config into temp build directories
  • Legacy line-of-business tools installed to a per-user AppData location with a bundled config
Suppression filter
| where WriterProcess !in~ ("dotnet.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe","testhost.exe","vstest.console.exe") and WriterPath !contains @"\Visual Studio"
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the flagged .exe.config and check for appDomainManagerAssembly/appDomainManagerType (or a legacyCorruptedState/startup redirect) plus a sibling unsigned DLL — those confirm AppDomainManager hijacking; also note the sibling .exe's signer. 2) Contain: isolate the host, block the sibling assembly hash, and preserve the folder for IR. 3) Hunt: pivot to the .NET host process executing from that folder, look for MiniUpdate/MiniJunk V2 C2 (including Azure-fronted beacons), and search other hosts for the same recruitment-lure delivery path.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where FolderPath !contains @"\Microsoft\" and FolderPath !contains @"\Programs\"
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe","dotnet.exe","setup.exe","officeclicktorun.exe","vs_installer.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, ConfigPath=FolderPath, ConfigFile=FileName, WriterProcess=InitiatingProcessFileName, WriterPath=InitiatingProcessFolderPath, WriterCmd=InitiatingProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFileName endswith ".exe.config"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\ProgramData\", @"\Users\Public\")
| where TargetFilePath !contains @"\Microsoft\" and TargetFilePath !contains @"\Programs\"
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("msiexec.exe","devenv.exe","msbuild.exe","dotnet.exe","setup.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine

Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time

    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time

         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",

Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process

Open-Source Android AI Agents Could Let Invisible Screen Text Run Code on Host PCs

The Hacker News
2026-07-21 14 use cases 7 techniques 4 kill-chain phases detected

An Android app that can draw over other windows and write to shared storage can slip instructions to the AI agent driving that phone, in text no human eye will ever see. Two more steps, and the same app is running commands on the PC driving the agent. Researchers demonstrated that chain, plus six other attacks, against five open-source mobile agent frameworks: AppAgent, AppAgentX,

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] Unauthenticated ADB keyboard broadcast (ADB_INPUT_B64 / ADB_INPUT_TEXT) from agent host · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] Host command injection via AppAgent 'adb shell input text' with shell metacharacters · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Fake CAPTCHA / clipboard-injected PowerShell (ClickFix / FakeCaptcha) · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Mobile-agent host RCE artifact: 'rce_success' file written by adb/python driver · Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
Host command injection via AppAgent 'adb shell input text' with shell metacharacters AIExploitation High
Hunts the article's escalation: a mobile-agent framework (AppAgent/AppAgentX/Mobile-Agent-v3/MobA) runs subprocess.run(adb_command, shell=True) and drops model-read screen text straight into 'adb shell input text {input_str}'. Because the live code only strips spaces/single-quotes, ';' '&' '>' survive and the back-half of the string executes on the operator's Windows box. This fires on an adb 'input text' command line that carries un-stripped shell metacharacters. Rationale: Uses the article's exact escalation primitive ('adb shell input text' + surviving ';' '&' '>' metacharacters from subprocess.run(shell=True)). A benign agent typing UI text never needs shell metacharacters in an input-text command, so the metacharacter clause is the high-fidelity differentiator. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00333v1 • https://arxiv.org/pdf/2607.00333
ATT&CKT1059.003 T1203
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Developer/QA manually typing test strings containing '&' or '>' via adb during app testing
  • Automation scripts that legitimately chain adb commands with '&' on one line (rare in input text context)
  • Password-fill automation that types special characters into a field via input text
  • A UI test that types a URL containing '>' or '|' as literal text
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessCommandLine has_any ("pytest","appium","uiautomator") and AccountName endswith "-qa")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full ProcessCommandLine and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — identify the back-half command after the metacharacter and whether it is a Windows binary (calc.exe, cmd.exe, powershell). Confirm the parent is a mobile-agent framework (python running AppAgent/AppAgentX/MobA). 2) Contain: kill the agent process, disconnect the phone (adb disconnect), and disable USB/wireless debugging on the paired device; isolate the host if a non-adb child process executed. 3) Hunt: search the same host for child processes spawned off the injected command, creation of files like 'rce_success', and any outbound connections from those children; review earlier screenshots pulled to /sdcard for attacker-planted overlay text.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "adb" and ProcessCommandLine has "input text"
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)input\s+text[^\r\n]*[;&|><]"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("python.exe","pythonw.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe","adb.exe","conhost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "adb" and CommandLine has "input text"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)input\s+text.*[;&|><]"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: ADB Input Text Command Injection via Shell Metacharacters
id: 5c2f9b41-8a7e-4d3c-9b1f-2e6a4c1d7f80
description: Detects an 'adb shell input text' command that carries un-sanitized shell metacharacters, matching the AppAgent mobile-agent host command-injection chain (arXiv 2607.00333).
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/open-source-android-ai-agents-could-let.html
  - https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00333v1
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:

  - attack.t1203
logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_adb:
    CommandLine|contains|all:
      - 'adb'
      - 'input text'
  selection_meta:
    CommandLine|re: '(?i)input\s+text.*[;&|><]'
  condition: selection_adb and selection_meta
level: high
source:(windows.security OR windows.sysmon) (@CommandLine:*adb* AND @CommandLine:*input\ text*) AND (@CommandLine:*\;* OR @CommandLine:*\&* OR @CommandLine:*\>* OR @CommandLine:*\|*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2
| CommandLine=/adb\s+.*input\s+text[^\r\n]*[;&|><]/i
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ParentBaseFileName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*adb*" AND Processes.process="*input text*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)input\s+text[^\r\n]*[;&|><]" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user parent_process_name process_name process count
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process="*adb*" AND Processes.process="*input text*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.parent_process Processes.process_name Processes.process | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | regex process="(?i)input\s+text[^\r\n]*[;&|><]" | `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)` | table firstTime lastTime dest user parent_process_name process_name process count
Mobile-agent host RCE artifact: 'rce_success' file written by adb/python driver AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the successful-injection marker from the paper's end-to-end AppAgent run, which used 'test;pwd>rce_success' to redirect the host working directory into a file named rce_success. Detects that file (or the redirect output) being created on the operator host by the adb/python agent process — a direct sign the command-injection chain landed code execution. Rationale: 'rce_success' is the paper's literal end-to-end PoC output filename ('test;pwd>rce_success'), written by the adb/python driver on the host — an unambiguous, article-specific artifact of a landed injection. Marked Medium confidence because it is a lab PoC string a real attacker could rename. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00333v1
ATT&CKT1059.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • A security team replaying the arXiv PoC in a sanctioned test lab
  • A researcher benchmarking agent frameworks with the paper's exact payload
  • A file legitimately named rce_success* created for unrelated reasons (extremely unlikely)
  • Backup/AV quarantine copies of a previously flagged rce_success file
Response runbook
1) Triage: open the rce_success file's parent folder and InitiatingProcessCommandLine — confirm it contains the injection payload (e.g. 'input text test;pwd>rce_success') and identify what the redirected command produced. 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the agent/python process, disconnect and re-image the paired phone if a malicious app is suspected, and disable ADB debugging. 3) Hunt: pivot to UC1 on the same host/user to find the injecting command line, enumerate every child process off the agent process, and check whether the same phone fed tampered screenshots to other paired hosts.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType in ("FileCreated","FileModified")
| where FileName startswith "rce_success"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName has_any ("adb.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, FolderPath, FileName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName startswith "rce_success"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("adb.exe","python.exe","pythonw.exe","cmd.exe","powershell.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ActorUsername
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: Mobile-Agent Command-Injection Success Marker rce_success File Write
id: 9f14a3c2-6b8d-4e1a-a2c7-51d0e93b4f6a

Unauthenticated ADB keyboard broadcast (ADB_INPUT_B64 / ADB_INPUT_TEXT) from agent host AIDelivery Low
Inventory/hunting rule for the article's 'nobody authenticated the keyboard' channel: Open-AutoGLM base64-encodes typed text to the implicit broadcast ADB_INPUT_B64, and Mobile-Agent-v3/MobA fall back to ADB_INPUT_TEXT for any non-ASCII character. Surfaces hosts issuing 'am broadcast -a ADB_INPUT_B64/ADB_INPUT_TEXT' so the SOC can find vulnerable agent deployments where any unprivileged app could intercept the same payload. Rationale: Matches the article's exact implicit-broadcast action strings (ADB_INPUT_B64, ADB_INPUT_TEXT) used by ADB Keyboard as the input plumbing. Low confidence because this is normal-but-insecure framework behaviour rather than an attack itself — value is fleet inventory of exploitable agent hosts, not per-event alerting. Cross-checked against: • https://arxiv.org/html/2607.00333v1
ATT&CKT1516 T1559
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate Open-AutoGLM / Mobile-Agent-v3 / MobA operation typing non-ASCII text (this is the framework's normal path)
  • QA teams using the ADB Keyboard test-automation tool as intended
  • Appium/uiautomator test suites broadcasting input via ADB Keyboard
  • Any developer intentionally using ADB Keyboard for IME testing
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm which framework issued the broadcast and whether the paired phone has other apps registered for the same intent action (on-device check) — the risk is interception, not the broadcast itself. 2) Contain: for production/sensitive hosts, migrate the framework to explicit intents or a signature-permission-protected input path, and audit the phone for unexpected apps holding no-permission broadcast receivers. 3) Hunt: correlate these hosts with UC1/UC2 to see if any also show injection metacharacters or rce_success artifacts, and inventory all endpoints running these five frameworks for patch/config remediation.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "broadcast"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("ADB_INPUT_B64","ADB_INPUT_TEXT")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(Timestamp), LastSeen=max(Timestamp), Count=count(), SampleCmd=any(ProcessCommandLine) by DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName
| order by FirstSeen desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "broadcast"
| where CommandLine has_any ("ADB_INPUT_B64","ADB_INPUT_TEXT")
| summarize FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated), LastSeen=max(TimeGenerated), Count=count(), SampleCmd=any(CommandLine) by Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName
| order by FirstSeen desc

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'

falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime

    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]

Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`

LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

New Bit2Watt Attack Could Let Cloud Tenants Disrupt Power Grids Without an Exploit

The Hacker News
2026-07-21 10 use cases 7 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

A cloud tenant using nothing but ordinary GPU access can push a data center's power draw up and down fast enough to threaten the grid it runs on, with no exploit and no break-in. That is the claim behind Bit2Watt, described by three Zhejiang University researchers in a paper accepted to CHES 2026, the IACR's hardware-security conference, and the evidence splits in two: they measured the power

ATT&CKT1021.001 T1190 T1195.002 T1486 T1528 T1555.003 T1566

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → Suspicious browser extension installation
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking.
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
