LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin credentialed read of /documents or /query (data exfil) AIActions on Objectives Medium
Hunts credentialed cross-origin HTTP requests to LightRAG's sensitive API endpoints (/documents, /query, /query/data) where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host — the exploitation signature of the CORS wildcard + allow_credentials flaw. A malicious site the victim visits rides their authenticated session to exfiltrate documents and knowledge-graph data. Rationale: Anchored on LightRAG's article-named endpoints (/login, /documents) plus /query corroborated by the official API docs, combined with the CORS root cause: the exploit necessarily produces a credentialed request whose Referer/Origin host != the LightRAG host. Comparing referer-host to target-host is the highest-fidelity behavioural signal the flaw leaves in access logs. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1185 T1213
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Split frontend/backend deployment where the LightRAG SPA is served from a different host/subdomain than the API, so legitimate reads carry a cross-origin Referer
  • API gateway or reverse proxy that rewrites Host, making Referer host legitimately differ from the logged CsHost
  • Grafana/BI dashboards or internal wikis embedding LightRAG query results with their own Referer
  • Swagger UI / ReDoc API console hosted on a separate documentation host
  • DAST scanners (Burp, OWASP ZAP) issuing requests with crafted Referer values
Suppression filter
| extend RefDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(RefererHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | extend TgtDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(TargetHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | where RefDomain != TgtDomain
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the offending RefererHost and CIp; confirm it is NOT a sanctioned internal frontend/gateway for this LightRAG instance and check whether the CsUsername session was concurrently active from a normal client. 2) Contain: set CORS_ORIGINS to an explicit allow-list (or allow_credentials=False) and upgrade lightrag-hku to >=1.5.4; if the RefererHost is an unknown external domain, block it at the proxy/WAF and force-invalidate active LightRAG tokens. 3) Hunt: sweep all LightRAG access logs for the same RefererHost across /documents, /query, /query/data and DELETE /documents; review volume of documents/knowledge-graph rows read to scope data exposure.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsUriStem has_any ("/documents", "/query")
| where CsMethod in ("GET","POST")
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer != "-"
| extend RefererHost = tolower(tostring(parse_url(Referer).Host))
| extend TargetHost = tolower(tostring(split(CsHost, ":")[0]))
| where isnotempty(RefererHost) and RefererHost != TargetHost
| where RefererHost !in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsUsername, CsMethod, CsUriStem, Referer, RefererHost, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

LightRAG CVE-2026-61736: cross-origin DELETE of document store (destructive CORS abuse) AIActions on Objectives High
Alerts on a credentialed cross-origin DELETE against LightRAG's /documents endpoints where the Referer/Origin host differs from the LightRAG host. The advisory calls out 'deleting the entire document store' as a destructive impact of the wildcard-CORS-with-credentials flaw; a DELETE riding the victim's session from an external origin is high-fidelity data destruction. Rationale: Uses the article's explicitly stated destructive impact (delete the document store) mapped to LightRAG's real DELETE /documents and DELETE /documents/delete_document endpoints (confirmed in the API-server docs), qualified by the cross-origin Referer signature that only the CORS flaw produces — a very low-FP, high-severity combination. Cross-checked against: • https://www.thehackerwire.com/lightrag-critical-credentialed-cors-vulnerability/ • https://github.com/HKUDS/LightRAG/blob/main/docs/LightRAG-API-Server.md • https://cve.threatint.eu/CVE/CVE-2026-61736
ATT&CKT1485 T1185
Data sourcesWeb.Web
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Admin performing bulk document deletion from a dedicated management console hosted on a different host than the API
  • Scheduled data-retention / cleanup jobs invoked from an orchestration host whose Referer differs from the API host
  • QA/staging teardown scripts that clear the document store between test runs
  • Split frontend deployment where the admin UI legitimately lives on another subdomain
Suppression filter
| extend RefDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(RefererHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | extend TgtDomain = strcat_array(array_slice(split(TargetHost,"."), -2, -1), ".") | where RefDomain != TgtDomain
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the RefererHost, CIp and CsUsername on the DELETE; verify whether an authorized admin intentionally cleared documents from a sanctioned console — if not, treat as active destruction. 2) Contain: immediately restrict CORS_ORIGINS to an explicit allow-list (or disable allow_credentials) and upgrade to lightrag-hku >=1.5.4; revoke/rotate the affected user's LightRAG token and, if data loss occurred, initiate restore of the document/KG store from backup. 3) Hunt: search for the same RefererHost/CIp across GET /documents and /query (pre-deletion reconnaissance/exfil) and for any /login POSTs from the same origin to establish the full session-riding chain.
AppServiceHTTPLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where CsMethod == "DELETE"
| where CsUriStem has "/documents"
| where isnotempty(Referer) and Referer != "-"

| where RefererHost !in ("localhost", "127.0.0.1")
| project TimeGenerated, CsHost, CIp, CsUsername, CsMethod, CsUriStem, Referer, RefererHost, UserAgent, ScStatus
| order by TimeGenerated desc

FakeGit Campaign Uses 7,600 GitHub Repositories to Spread SmartLoader Malware

The Hacker News
2026-07-20 16 use cases 9 techniques 5 kill-chain phases detected

Cybersecurity researchers have discovered nearly 7,600 malicious GitHub repositories, out of which more than 800 pose as artificial intelligence (AI) skills or Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers to deliver a malware family known as SmartLoader as part of an ongoing campaign codenamed FakeGit. "FakeGit uses copied projects, lookalike developer profiles, convincing READMEs, and malicious ZIP

Actions on Objectives
Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration.
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] SmartLoader LuaJIT loader chain: luajit.exe/Compiler.exe executing userdata.txt Lua script · [LLM] SmartLoader persistence: LuaJIT runtime copied to %AppData%\ODE3 (module.class/lua51.dll) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] SmartLoader blockchain C2: non-browser process resolving pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon eth_call dead-drop · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
SmartLoader LuaJIT loader chain: luajit.exe/Compiler.exe executing userdata.txt Lua script AIInstallation High
Hunts the FakeGit SmartLoader install stage where a batch launcher spawns a LuaJIT runtime (luajit.exe / Compiler.exe / renamed ODE3.exe) that loads lua51.dll and executes an obfuscated single-line Lua script passed as a .txt/.log argument from a user-writable path. This is the specific delivery-to-execution pivot of the counterfeit GitHub-repo ZIP, not generic script execution. Rationale: Anchors on the exact SmartLoader ZIP components (luajit.exe/Compiler.exe/ODE3.exe + userdata.txt) confirmed across Trend Micro, Hexastrike and ASEC write-ups; a LuaJIT interpreter running a .txt/.log script from Downloads/Temp/AppData is not a normal software pattern. Cross-checked against: • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/ • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/89551/
ATT&CKT1204.002 T1059 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate game or app bundling LuaJIT that ships a .log config in its own install dir (rare in Downloads/Temp)
  • Developer running luajit.exe against a .txt test script from a project folder under AppData
  • Redistributable installers extracting to %Temp% that legitimately embed lua51.dll
  • Security researcher detonating the sample in a lab
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("devenv.exe","steam.exe") and FolderPath has @"\Program Files")
Response runbook
1) Triage: pull the full process tree — confirm parent is Launcher.bat/cmd.exe and that lua51.dll loaded from the same user-writable folder; hash the luajit.exe and .txt script and check size (SmartLoader Lua scripts are ~296-309 KB single-line). 2) Contain: isolate the host, kill the luajit/ODE3 process tree, and block the source GitHub release URL if recoverable from FileOriginUrl. 3) Hunt: search the same host for %AppData%\ODE3 drops and a 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3' scheduled task (UC2) and outbound C2 to pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon RPC (UC3) to confirm SmartLoader→StealC progression.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","ODE3.exe") or InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("userdata.txt",".txt",".log")
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\") or InitiatingProcessFolderPath has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where not(TargetUserName endswith "$")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","ODE3.exe") or ParentProcessName has_any ("luajit.exe","Compiler.exe","Launcher.bat")
| where CommandLine has_any ("userdata.txt",".txt",".log")
| where CommandLine has_any (@"\Downloads\", @"\Temp\", @"\AppData\", @"\Public\")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, NewProcessName, CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: SmartLoader LuaJIT Runtime Executing Text-File Lua Script
id: 6f3a1c8e-9d21-4b77-8f1a-2c4e5b7a9d10
description: Detects FakeGit/SmartLoader LuaJIT loader chain where luajit.exe or a renamed copy executes an obfuscated .txt/.log Lua script from a user-writable path
references:
  - https://thehackernews.com/2026/07/fakegit-campaign-uses-7600-github.html
  - https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html
  - https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/
author: SOC Detection Engineering
date: 2026/07/21
tags:
  - attack.t1204.002

logsource:
  category: process_creation
  product: windows
detection:
  selection_img:
    Image|endswith:
      - '\luajit.exe'
      - '\Compiler.exe'
      - '\ODE3.exe'

    CommandLine|contains:

      - '.log'
  selection_path:

      - '\Temp\'
      - '\AppData\'

  condition: selection_img and selection_arg and selection_path
level: high
source:windows.sysmon @EventID:1 @Image:(*\\luajit.exe OR *\\Luajit.exe OR *\\LUAJIT.EXE OR *\\Compiler.exe OR *\\compiler.exe OR *\\ODE3.exe OR *\\ode3.exe) @CommandLine:(*userdata.txt* OR *.txt* OR *.log*) @CommandLine:(*\\Downloads\\* OR *\\Temp\\* OR *\\AppData\\* OR *\\Public\\*)
#event_simpleName=ProcessRollup2 ImageFileName=/\\(luajit|compiler|ode3)\.exe$/i
| CommandLine=/(userdata\.txt|\.txt|\.log)/i
| regex("(?i)\\\\(Downloads|Temp|AppData|Public)\\\\", field=CommandLine)
| groupBy([aid, ComputerName, ImageFileName, CommandLine], function=count())
ENDPOINT

| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes where (Processes.process_name IN ("luajit.exe","compiler.exe","ODE3.exe") OR Processes.parent_process_name IN ("luajit.exe","compiler.exe","launcher.bat")) (Processes.process="*userdata.txt*" OR Processes.process="*.txt*" OR Processes.process="*.log*") by Processes.dest Processes.user Processes.parent_process_name Processes.process_name Processes.process Processes.parent_process Processes.process_path | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)` | where match(process_path,"(?i)\\(Downloads|Temp|AppData|Public)\\") | sort - lastTime
SmartLoader persistence: LuaJIT runtime copied to %AppData%\ODE3 (module.class/lua51.dll) AIInstallation High
Detects the SmartLoader persistence stage that copies the renamed LuaJIT runtime (ODE3.exe), a module.class blob, and lua51.dll into %AppData%\Roaming\ODE3, later registered as scheduled task 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3'. The module.class filename beside lua51.dll in a per-user Roaming folder is a highly specific FakeGit artifact. Rationale: module.class + lua51.dll + ODE3.exe co-located in %AppData%\ODE3 is the exact persistence artifact documented by intellibron/ASEC; requiring >=2 of the three artifacts in the same folder near-eliminates coincidental hits. Cross-checked against: • https://blog.intellibron.io/lua-jit-smartloader-analyzing-the-github-campaign-delivering-stealer/ • https://asec.ahnlab.com/en/89551/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html
ATT&CKT1053.005 T1036.005 T1547.001
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • An unrelated legitimate app that happens to use an 'ODE3' product folder (uncommon)
  • Backup/sync tools (OneDrive, Dropbox) replicating a previously-infected AppData tree — writer will be the sync client, not luajit
  • Analyst restoring quarantined files during IR (writer = AV/EDR)
  • Java-based app writing a real module.class but NOT alongside lua51.dll in an ODE3 folder (the >=2 artifact gate filters this)
Suppression filter
| where Writer !in~ ("onedrive.exe","dropbox.exe","googledrivefs.exe","MsMpEng.exe")
Response runbook
1) Triage: confirm the writing process (InitiatingProcessFileName) is luajit.exe/Compiler.exe rather than a sync client; enumerate the ODE3 folder contents and check for a 'SecurityHealthService_ODE3' scheduled task (schtasks /query or DeviceEvents ScheduledTaskCreated). 2) Contain: isolate host, delete the scheduled task, remove %AppData%\ODE3, and kill any running ODE3.exe. 3) Hunt: pivot to the loader-chain execution (UC1) to find the originating ZIP and to C2 telemetry (UC3) for pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon RPC beaconing indicating StealC staging.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ActionType == "FileCreated"
| where FolderPath has @"\ODE3\"
| where FileName in~ ("ODE3.exe","module.class","lua51.dll")
| summarize Artifacts=make_set(FileName), Writer=any(InitiatingProcessFileName), WriterCmd=any(InitiatingProcessCommandLine), FirstSeen=min(Timestamp) by DeviceName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessAccountName
| where array_length(Artifacts) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventType == "FileCreated"
| where TargetFilePath has @"\ODE3\"
| where TargetFileName in~ ("ODE3.exe","module.class","lua51.dll")
| summarize Artifacts=make_set(TargetFileName), Writer=any(ActingProcessName), FirstSeen=min(TimeGenerated) by DvcHostname, TargetFilePath, ActorUsername
| where array_length(Artifacts) >= 2
| order by FirstSeen desc

SmartLoader blockchain C2: non-browser process resolving pasteflawwed[.]world / Polygon eth_call dead-drop AICommand & Control High
Detects SmartLoader command-and-control where the LuaJIT runtime (luajit.exe/ODE3.exe/Compiler.exe) beacons to the FakeGit C2 domain pasteflawwed[.]world or issues JSON-RPC eth_call requests to public Polygon RPC endpoints to retrieve the next-stage StealC payload from a smart-contract dead-drop resolver. Rationale: pasteflawwed[.]world is the named SmartLoader C2 domain and the Polygon eth_call dead-drop resolver is the campaign's documented blockchain C2 (Trend Micro/Hexastrike); gating the RPC endpoints on a luajit/ODE3 initiating process avoids flagging legitimate crypto tooling. Cross-checked against: • https://hexastrike.com/resources/blog/threat-intelligence/cloned-loaded-and-stolen-how-109-fake-github-repositories-delivered-smartloader-and-stealc/ • https://www.planetjon.net/news/cybersecurity/smartloader-stealc-campaign-blockchain-c2-and-fraudulent-github-repositories/ • https://www.trendmicro.com/en_us/research/25/c/ai-assisted-fake-github-repositories.html
ATT&CKT1102.001 T1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Resolution.DNS
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate web3/DeFi developer wallet or MetaMask backend resolving Polygon RPC (initiating process is a browser/node, not luajit — excluded by the process gate)
  • Blockchain analytics or node software polling rpc.ankr.com from a server
  • Threat-intel or sandbox appliance resolving pasteflawwed[.]world during analysis
  • DNS sinkhole / security proxy re-resolving the IOC for blocking
Suppression filter
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","node.exe","metamask.exe") or RemoteUrl has "pasteflawwed.world"
Response runbook
1) Triage: identify the process behind the DNS/connection — in Defender confirm InitiatingProcessFileName is luajit.exe/ODE3.exe; a LuaJIT runtime issuing eth_call JSON-RPC is not legitimate. 2) Contain: isolate host, block pasteflawwed[.]world and the abused Polygon RPC FQDNs at egress, and kill/quarantine the ODE3 process tree. 3) Hunt: correlate back to the ODE3 persistence folder and scheduled task (UC2) and the original loader execution (UC1); sweep other hosts for the same C2 resolution and check for StealC exfil (credential-store access, browser DB reads) following the beacon.
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where (RemoteUrl has "pasteflawwed.world")
    or (InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("luajit.exe","ODE3.exe","Compiler.exe")
        and RemoteUrl has_any ("polygon-rpc.com","polygon.llamarpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon.drpc.org"))
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, RemoteUrl, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| order by Timestamp desc
ImDnsActivity
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where DnsQuery has_any ("pasteflawwed.world","polygon-rpc.com","polygon.llamarpc.com","rpc.ankr.com","polygon.drpc.org")
| project TimeGenerated, SrcIpAddr, SrcHostname, DnsQuery, DnsResponseName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs Actions on Objectives High
Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies SQLite from Chrome/Edge/Firefox.
ATT&CKT1539 T1555.003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where FolderPath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\", @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\", @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FolderPath, FileName, ActionType

// ASIM ImFileEvent — covers MDE, Sysmon, AuditD, Defender for Cloud, etc.
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where TargetFilePath has_any (@"\Google\Chrome\User Data\",
                                  @"\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\",
                                  @"\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\")
| where TargetFileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where ActingProcessName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName,
          TargetFilePath, TargetFileName, EventType

title: Infostealer - Non-Browser Process Accessing Browser Credential Stores
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |
    Stealers (RedLine, Lumma, Vidar, Atomic) read Login Data / cookies
    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1539/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1555/003/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1539
    - attack.t1555.003
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: file_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_path:
        TargetFilename|contains:
            - '\Google\Chrome\User Data\'
            - '\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\'
            - '\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\'
    selection_file:
        TargetFilename|endswith:
            - '\Login Data'
            - '\Cookies'
            - '\logins.json'
            - '\cookies.sqlite'
    filter_browser:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\chrome.exe'
            - '\msedge.exe'
            - '\firefox.exe'
            - '\brave.exe'
            - '\opera.exe'
    condition: selection_path and selection_file and not filter_browser
falsepositives:
    - Backup utilities reading user profile files
    - Browser sync agents from non-stock vendors
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where (Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Google\Chrome\User Data\*\Cookies*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Microsoft\Edge\User Data\*\Login Data*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\logins.json*"
        OR Filesystem.file_path="*\Mozilla\Firefox\Profiles\*\cookies.sqlite*")
      AND NOT Filesystem.process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.process_name, Filesystem.file_path, Filesystem.user
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution Delivery High
User received an external email containing a URL, clicked it, and within 60 seconds the recipient's endpoint spawned a scripting interpreter or network downloader (PowerShell / cmd / mshta / curl / certutil / bitsadmin). This is the high-fidelity shape — a raw "user clicked an emailed URL" query is too noisy to alert on because every Microsoft 365 tenant generates thousands of legitimate clicks per day. The exec-correlation step suppresses the noise to roughly the rate at which a click actually drives onto-host execution, which is the actionable signal. Pair with UC_PHISH_LINK_BYPASS (Safe Links override) and UC_PHISH_LINK_NEWDOMAIN for orthogonal high-fidelity variants.
ATT&CKT1566.002 T1204.001 T1059.001
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Web Endpoint.Processes EmailEvents EmailUrlInfo UrlClickEvents DeviceProcessEvents
// Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s.
// Far higher fidelity than "every clicked URL" — most legitimate clicks
// never spawn a non-browser child process, so the join eliminates the
// 99% of noise that makes a raw click query unactionable.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectClicks = UrlClickEvents
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | where ActionType in ("ClickAllowed","ClickedThrough")
    | join kind=inner (
        EmailEvents
        | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
        | where DeliveryAction == "Delivered"
        | where EmailDirection == "Inbound"
        | project NetworkMessageId, Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain,
                  RecipientEmailAddress, EmailTimestamp = Timestamp
      ) on NetworkMessageId
    | join kind=leftouter (
        EmailUrlInfo | project NetworkMessageId, Url, UrlDomain
      ) on NetworkMessageId, Url
    | project ClickTime = Timestamp, AccountUpn, IPAddress, Url, UrlDomain,
              Subject, SenderFromAddress, SenderFromDomain, RecipientEmailAddress,
              ActionType;
// Correlate to a non-browser child process spawned within 60 seconds on
// the recipient's device.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                         "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                        "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                        "bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe","curl.exe","wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectClicks on $left.AccountName == $right.AccountUpn
| where Timestamp between (ClickTime .. ClickTime + 60s)
| project ClickTime, ProcessTime = Timestamp,
          DelaySec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, ClickTime),
          DeviceName, AccountName, RecipientEmailAddress, SenderFromAddress,
          Subject, Url, UrlDomain, ActionType,
          FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by ClickTime desc
// UrlClickEvents has no clean Sentinel-native equivalent. The detection
// pivots to: Office Send→Receive proximity to SecurityEvent 4688 of a
// non-browser child process. Lower fidelity than the Defender version.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let SuspectMailUsers = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation =~ "Receive"
    | summarize Subject = any(Subject), Sender = any(Sender)
                by MailboxOwnerUPN, MessageId, EmailTime = bin(TimeGenerated, 1m);
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("\chrome.exe","\msedge.exe",
                                     "\firefox.exe","\outlook.exe","\brave.exe")
| where NewProcessName has_any ("\powershell.exe","\pwsh.exe","\cmd.exe",
                                  "\mshta.exe","\rundll32.exe","\regsvr32.exe",
                                  "\wscript.exe","\cscript.exe","\bitsadmin.exe",
                                  "\certutil.exe","\curl.exe","\wget.exe")
| join kind=inner SuspectMailUsers on $left.Account == $right.MailboxOwnerUPN
| where TimeGenerated between (EmailTime .. EmailTime + 60s)
| project TimeGenerated, EmailTime, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine, Sender, Subject
| order by TimeGenerated desc
WEB
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats `summariesonly` earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
``` Phishing-link click that drives endpoint execution within 60s ```
| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS click_time
    from datamodel=Web
    where Web.action="allowed"
    by Web.src, Web.user, Web.dest, Web.url
| `drop_dm_object_name(Web)`
| rename user AS recipient, dest AS clicked_domain, url AS clicked_url
| join type=inner recipient
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
         from datamodel=Email.All_Email
         where All_Email.action="delivered" AND All_Email.url!="-"
         by All_Email.recipient, All_Email.src_user, All_Email.url, All_Email.subject
     | `drop_dm_object_name(All_Email)`
     | rex field=url "https?://(?<email_domain>[^/]+)"
     | rename recipient AS recipient]
| join type=inner src
    [| tstats summariesonly=false earliest(_time) AS exec_time
         values(Processes.process) AS exec_cmd, values(Processes.process_name) AS exec_proc
         from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
         where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe",
                                                   "outlook.exe","brave.exe","arc.exe")
           AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","cmd.exe","mshta.exe",
                                            "rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wscript.exe",
                                            "cscript.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe",
                                            "curl.exe","wget.exe")
         by Processes.dest, Processes.user
     | `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
     | rename dest AS src]
| eval delta_sec = exec_time - click_time
| where delta_sec >= 0 AND delta_sec <= 60
| table click_time, exec_time, delta_sec, recipient, src, src_user, subject,
        clicked_domain, clicked_url, exec_proc, exec_cmd
| sort - click_time
Email attachment opened from external sender Delivery High
Attachment delivery + execution by recipient — most common malware initial access.
ATT&CKT1566.001 T1204.002
Data sourcesEmail.All_Email Endpoint.Processes EmailAttachmentInfo DeviceProcessEvents
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MalAttachments = EmailAttachmentInfo
    | where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where AccountName !endswith "$"
    | project NetworkMessageId, RecipientEmailAddress,
              AttachmentFileName = FileName, AttachmentSHA256 = SHA256;
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(LookbackDays)
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe",
                      "mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
| join kind=inner MalAttachments on $left.AccountUpn == $right.RecipientEmailAddress
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, AttachmentFileName, AttachmentSHA256
// Sentinel doesn't have an attachment-hash table. Best approximation:
// OfficeActivity Send/Receive activity + correlate to host process spawn.
let LookbackDays = 7d;
let MailWithAttach = OfficeActivity
    | where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
    | where OfficeWorkload == "Exchange"
    | where Operation in~ ("Send","Receive")
    | where isnotempty(MessageId)
    | project EmailTime = TimeGenerated, MailboxOwnerUPN, Sender,
              Recipients, Subject, MessageId;
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(LookbackDays)
| where EventID == 4688
| where ParentProcessName endswith "OUTLOOK.EXE"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats `summariesonly` count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
| tstats summariesonly=false count
    from datamodel=Email.All_Email
    where All_Email.file_name!="-"
    by All_Email.src_user, All_Email.recipient, All_Email.file_name, All_Email.subject
| rename All_Email.recipient as user
| join type=inner user
    [| tstats summariesonly=false count
        from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
        where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("OUTLOOK.EXE","winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe")
          AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe")
        by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
     | rename Processes.user as user]
Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process Exploitation High
Classic macro/exploit pattern — Office app launching cmd/powershell/wmic/regsvr32.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1059.005 T1218
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName endswith "\winword.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\excel.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\powerpnt.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\outlook.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\onenote.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\mspub.exe"
   or ParentProcessName endswith "\visio.exe"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"

title: Office Application Spawning Script Host
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d07
status: experimental
description: |
    Word/Excel/Outlook/OneNote spawning powershell, cmd, wscript,
    cscript, mshta, rundll32, regsvr32 — classic macro / embedded-
    object payload signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1566/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059
    - attack.t1566.001
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_parent:
        ParentImage|endswith:
            - '\winword.exe'
            - '\excel.exe'
            - '\powerpnt.exe'
            - '\outlook.exe'
            - '\onenote.exe'
            - '\mspub.exe'
            - '\visio.exe'
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
    condition: selection_parent and selection_child
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate automation macros in trusted internal documents
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.parent_process_name IN ("winword.exe","excel.exe","powerpnt.exe","outlook.exe","onenote.exe","mspub.exe","visio.exe")
      AND Processes.process_name IN ("cmd.exe","powershell.exe","pwsh.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","mshta.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe","certutil.exe")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.parent_process_name, Processes.process_name, Processes.process
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| `security_content_ctime(firstTime)` | `security_content_ctime(lastTime)`
OAuth consent / suspicious app grant Actions on Objectives High
Cloud identity abuse: app gets high-priv scopes, often via consent phishing.
ATT&CKT1528 T1098.001
Data sourcesAuthentication.Authentication CloudAppEvents
CloudAppEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where ActionType in ("Consent to application.","Add OAuth2PermissionGrant.","Add delegated permission grant.")
| project Timestamp, AccountObjectId, AccountDisplayName, ActivityType,
          ActivityObjects, IPAddress, UserAgent
// Entra ID directory audit — user / admin consent to a third-party app.
AuditLogs
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where OperationName has "Consent to application"
| where Result =~ "success"
| extend AppName = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].displayName),
         AppId   = tostring(parse_json(tostring(TargetResources))[0].id),
         User    = tostring(parse_json(tostring(InitiatedBy)).user.userPrincipalName)
| project TimeGenerated, OperationName, User, AppName, AppId, Result
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Entra ID Consent to Third-Party OAuth Application
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d05
status: experimental
description: |
    User-driven consent to a third-party OAuth application — illicit-
    consent attack precursor. Pair with first-time-seen-app heuristic
    in your SIEM for higher fidelity.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1528/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1528
    - attack.persistence
logsource:
    product: azure
    service: auditlogs
detection:
    selection:
        OperationName: 'Consent to application'
        Result: 'success'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:
    - Legitimate first-time SaaS app onboarding
level: medium
APPLICATION
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Authentication.Authentication
    where Authentication.action="success"
      AND Authentication.signature IN (
        "Consent to application",
        "Add app role assignment grant to user",
        "Add OAuth2PermissionGrant",
        "Add delegated permission grant")
    by Authentication.user, Authentication.app, Authentication.src, Authentication.signature
| `drop_dm_object_name(Authentication)`
PowerShell encoded / obfuscated command Exploitation High
Encoded or obfuscated PowerShell — common across loaders, recon, and post-exploitation.
ATT&CKT1059.001 T1027
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
| where ProcessCommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, ProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\pwsh.exe"
| where CommandLine matches regex @"(?i)(-enc|encodedcommand|frombase64string|-nop|-w\s+hidden|invoke-expression|iex\s*\(|downloadstring|net\.webclient)"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName,
          CommandLine, ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Obfuscated / Encoded PowerShell Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d08
status: experimental
description: |
    PowerShell launched with -EncodedCommand, base64 strings, hidden
    window, no-profile, bypass policy, IEX / Invoke-Expression / Net
    .WebClient.DownloadString — combinations indicating evasion.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1059/001/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1059.001
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.execution
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_image:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
    selection_args:
        CommandLine|contains:
            - '-enc '
            - 'EncodedCommand'
            - 'FromBase64String'
            - 'Invoke-Expression'
            - 'IEX('
            - 'DownloadString'
            - 'Net.WebClient'
            - '-w hidden'
            - '-WindowStyle Hidden'
            - '-nop'
            - '-NoProfile'
            - '-ep bypass'
            - '-ExecutionPolicy Bypass'
    condition: selection_image and selection_args
falsepositives:
    - DevOps tooling that legitimately uses encoded command for
      cross-shell escaping
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","pwsh.exe")
      AND (Processes.process="*-enc *" OR Processes.process="*EncodedCommand*"
        OR Processes.process="*FromBase64String*" OR Processes.process="*-nop*"
        OR Processes.process="*-w hidden*" OR Processes.process="*Invoke-Expression*"
        OR Processes.process="*IEX(*" OR Processes.process="*DownloadString*"
        OR Processes.process="*Net.WebClient*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change Actions on Objectives Medium
Threshold detection: many files renamed in short window, often with new extension.
ATT&CKT1486
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem DeviceFileEvents
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(FileName) by DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, bin(Timestamp, 1m)
| where files > 200    // empirical: > 200 unique-file renames in 1m by one account on one host
                       //            is well above the P99 of legitimate bulk-tooling
| order by files desc

ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where ActorUsername !endswith "$"
| where EventType in ("FileRenamed","FileModified")
| summarize files = dcount(TargetFileName)
            by DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, bin(TimeGenerated, 1m)
| where files > 200    // P99 of legit bulk-tooling per-minute rename volume
| order by files desc
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
| tstats summariesonly=false count, dc(Filesystem.file_name) AS files
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Filesystem
    where Filesystem.action IN ("modified","renamed")
    by Filesystem.dest, Filesystem.user, _time span=1m
| `drop_dm_object_name(Filesystem)`
| where files > 200
| sort - files
LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) Actions on Objectives High
Mimikatz, comsvcs.dll MiniDump, or any non-Windows process opening LSASS.
ATT&CKT1003.001 T1003
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceEvents
DeviceEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where ActionType == "OpenProcessApiCall"
| where FileName =~ "lsass.exe"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("MsSense.exe","MsMpEng.exe","csrss.exe",
                                          "svchost.exe","wininit.exe","services.exe",
                                          "lsm.exe","SearchProtocolHost.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, ActionType, FileName,
          InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessCommandLine,
          InitiatingProcessFolderPath, AccountName
| order by Timestamp desc
// SecurityEvent EventID 4663 = object access. AccessMask 0x10 / 0x40 / 0x1010
// indicate read access to lsass.exe — credential-dump signature. Audit
// Object Access > Audit File System policy required.
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4663
| where ObjectName endswith "\lsass.exe"
| where Account !endswith "$"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ObjectName, ProcessName,
          AccessMask, AccessReason
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: LSASS Process Access Outside Microsoft-Signed Tooling
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d04
status: experimental
description: |
    Anything opening lsass.exe with read-memory access that isn't a
    Microsoft signed component (Defender, csrss, etc.) is suspect.
    Mimikatz / Pypykatz / nanodump signature.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1003/001/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1003.001
    - attack.credential-access
logsource:
    category: process_access
    product: windows
detection:
    selection:
        TargetImage|endswith: '\lsass.exe'
    filter_known_good:
        SourceImage|endswith:
            - '\MsSense.exe'
            - '\MsMpEng.exe'
            - '\csrss.exe'
            - '\svchost.exe'
            - '\wininit.exe'
            - '\services.exe'
            - '\lsm.exe'
            - '\SearchProtocolHost.exe'
    condition: selection and not filter_known_good
falsepositives:
    - Third-party EDR / forensic tools — extend the filter list
level: high
ENDPOINT
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
| tstats summariesonly=false count min(_time) as firstTime max(_time) as lastTime
    from datamodel=Endpoint.Processes
    where (Processes.process="*lsass*" OR Processes.process="*sekurlsa*"
        OR Processes.process="*MiniDump*" OR Processes.process="*comsvcs.dll*MiniDump*"
        OR Processes.process="*procdump*lsass*")
       OR (Processes.process_name="rundll32.exe" AND Processes.process="*comsvcs*MiniDump*")
    by Processes.dest, Processes.user, Processes.process_name, Processes.process, Processes.parent_process_name
| `drop_dm_object_name(Processes)`
Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement Actions on Objectives High
psexec / paexec / smbexec / wmic /node — service install over SMB from remote host.
ATT&CKT1021.002 T1569.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where FileName in~ ("psexec.exe","psexesvc.exe","paexec.exe","smbexec.py")
   or (FileName =~ "wmic.exe" and ProcessCommandLine has "/node:")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine, InitiatingProcessFileName
| order by Timestamp desc

SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688            // process-create (audit-policy required)
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where NewProcessName endswith "\psexec.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\psexesvc.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\paexec.exe"
   or (NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe" and CommandLine has "/node:")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, NewProcessName, CommandLine,
          ParentProcessName
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: PsExec / SMB Lateral Movement Tooling Execution
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d03
status: experimental
description: |
    PsExec, paexec, smbexec, csexec, remcom — admin-grade tooling that
    pivots over SMB. Pair with `wmic /node:` for the full cluster.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1021/002/
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1569/002/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1021.002
    - attack.t1569.002
    - attack.lateral-movement
    - attack.execution
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows

            - '\psexec.exe'
            - '\psexec64.exe'
            - '\psexesvc.exe'
            - '\paexec.exe'
            - '\csexec.exe'
            - '\remcom.exe'
            - '\smbexec.py'

      a known-admin-host watchlist

Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children Exploitation Medium
Supply-chain trojan signal: legitimate signed binary spawning script interpreters or exotic LOLBins.
ATT&CKT1195.002
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes DeviceProcessEvents
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| where InitiatingProcessFileName in~ ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where FileName in~ ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
// Replace `"setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe"` with the vendor binaries observed in the
// article (matching shape with the Defender query).
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(7d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where Account !endswith "$"
| where ParentProcessName has_any ("setup.exe","installer.exe","update.exe")
| where NewProcessName endswith "\powershell.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cmd.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\rundll32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\regsvr32.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\mshta.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\cscript.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\wmic.exe"
   or NewProcessName endswith "\bitsadmin.exe"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, Account, ParentProcessName,
          NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

title: Trusted Vendor Binary Launching Unusual Children
id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d09
status: experimental
description: |
    A signed vendor binary (in the article's named-vendors list)
    spawning script-host or LOLBin children. Strongest signal when
    paired with a recent CVE / supply-chain advisory naming the same
    vendor.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1195/
author: Clankerusecase
date: 2026/05/02
tags:
    - attack.t1195
    - attack.initial-access
logsource:
    category: process_creation
    product: windows
detection:
    selection_child:
        Image|endswith:
            - '\powershell.exe'
            - '\pwsh.exe'
            - '\cmd.exe'
            - '\rundll32.exe'
            - '\regsvr32.exe'
            - '\mshta.exe'
            - '\wscript.exe'
            - '\cscript.exe'
            - '\wmic.exe'
            - '\bitsadmin.exe'
    selection_parent_vendor:
        ParentImage|contains:
            - '\Program Files\'
            - '\Program Files (x86)\'
    condition: selection_child and selection_parent_vendor
falsepositives:
    - Many — installers and updaters legitimately spawn children. Pin
      the parent path to specific vendor binaries observed in the
      article before alerting.
level: medium
ENDPOINT

      AND Processes.process_name IN ("powershell.exe","cmd.exe","rundll32.exe","regsvr32.exe","mshta.exe","wscript.exe","cscript.exe","wmic.exe","bitsadmin.exe")

title: File or Process Matching Article Hash IOCs

status: experimental
description: |
    Replace `__HASH_LIST__` placeholder with article-specific SHA256
    values. Use a watchlist or external indicator file for management
    at scale.
references:
    - https://attack.mitre.org/techniques/T1027/
author: Clankerusecase

tags:
    - attack.t1027
    - attack.defense-evasion
logsource:

    product: windows
detection:

        Hashes|contains:
            - 'SHA256=__HASH_PLACEHOLDER_REPLACE_ME__'
    condition: selection
falsepositives:

level: critical

Detected
Reconnaissance. Attacker researches the target — OSINT, scanning, enumeration. → Asset exposure — vulnerability matches article CVE(s)
Weaponization. Coupling exploit code with deliverable payload (e.g. weaponized PDF/Office doc, trojanized installer).
Delivery. Transmitting the weapon (phishing email, USB, watering hole, drive-by, malicious ad). → [LLM] search-ms: URI opening a remote WebDAV share filtered to .scr payloads · [LLM] RTLO / double-extension executable masquerading as a CURP PDF report · Phishing-link click correlated to endpoint execution · Email attachment opened from external sender
Exploitation. Triggering the exploit — vulnerability/macro/trust abuse to execute code. → [LLM] WebDAV working-directory hijack: signed binary spawns child from remote share (CVE-2025-33053) · Office app spawning script/LOLBin child process · Trusted vendor binary / installer launching unusual children · Article-specific behavioural hunt — Exposed Server Reveals AI-Assisted Phishing Toolkit Behind WebDAV Malware Campai
Installation. Establishing persistence on the host — backdoor, service, scheduled task, registry key. → [LLM] Signed Ubisoft-branded binary executing from a user-writable path (DlrtyGames DLL side-load) · Suspicious browser extension installation · File hash IOCs — endpoint file/process match
Command & Control. Beacon to attacker infrastructure for control and tasking. → [LLM] Known Simba Service WebDAV campaign C2 IPs, domains and payload hashes · Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations · Network connections to article IPs / domains
Actions on Objectives. Lateral movement, credential dumping, data theft, ransomware, sabotage. → Infostealer — non-browser process accessing browser cookie/login DBs · OAuth consent / suspicious app grant · Ransomware-style mass file rename / extension change · LSASS process access / dump (credential theft) · Remote service execution — PsExec / SMB lateral movement
WebDAV working-directory hijack: signed binary spawns child from remote share (CVE-2025-33053) AIExploitation High
Hunts the CVE-2025-33053 technique the operator reproduced: a .url shortcut launches a legitimate signed Windows binary (e.g. iediagcmd.exe) whose working directory points at an attacker WebDAV share, so a bare-filename helper like route.exe is loaded from the remote DavWWWRoot instead of System32. Detection keys on any process whose image path resolves to a WebDAV share (DavWWWRoot / @SSL@ crumbs), which is the article's core execution primitive. Rationale: Anchors on the exact WebDAV path markers (DavWWWRoot, @SSL@) that appear in the operator's recovered README example summerartcamp[.]net@ssl@443\DavWWWRoot\OSYxaOjr and in Check Point's original Stealth Falcon writeup of CVE-2025-33053 — any executable image resolving from a WebDAV share is anomalous. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/stealth-falcon-zero-day/ • https://www.cisa.gov/known-exploited-vulnerabilities-catalog
ATT&CKT1574.008 T1204.002 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Legitimate WebDAV-mounted document shares in enterprises that publish tools over SSL WebDAV
  • Sysinternals live.sysinternals.com WebDAV usage by admins running tools directly from the share
  • SharePoint/Office WebDAV drive redirection when opening Office binaries from a mapped SSL share
  • Backup or DMS agents that stage executables on a WebDAV endpoint
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessFolderPath has "sysinternals" and DeviceName in (dynamic([])))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Pull the parent process and command line — confirm a signed system binary (iediagcmd.exe, or one of the 59 candidate LOLBAS/.NET tools) launched a helper whose FolderPath is a remote DavWWWRoot/@SSL@ share; capture the WebDAV host and correlate to the C2 IOC list. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process tree, and block the WebDAV host at proxy/firewall; disable the WebClient service via GPO on at-risk fleets. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for .url files referencing @SSL@/DavWWWRoot, WebClient service starts, and davclnt.dll reaching external hosts across the estate.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FolderPath has "DavWWWRoot" or FolderPath has "@SSL@"
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, InitiatingProcessFolderPath, InitiatingProcessCommandLine, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where NewProcessName has "DavWWWRoot" or NewProcessName has "@SSL@"
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc

search-ms: URI opening a remote WebDAV share filtered to .scr payloads AIDelivery Medium
Hunts the delivery step where the gobf[.]mx CURP lookalike page's download button fired a search-ms: query that opened the operator's WebDAV share as an Explorer search filtered to .scr files. Detection keys on process command lines combining the search-ms: protocol handler with a remote WebDAV crumb, the article's specific initial-access mechanism. Rationale: The article explicitly states the download button fired a search-ms: query opening the WebDAV share filtered to .scr files; the search-ms:+WebDAV-crumb pairing is a high-fidelity, article-specific delivery artifact rarely seen in benign use. Cross-checked against: • https://research.checkpoint.com/2025/stealth-falcon-zero-day/
ATT&CKT1204.001 T1105
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Power users invoking saved Explorer searches (.search-ms) against internal file servers
  • Legitimate enterprise WebDAV document portals accessed via search connectors
  • IT scripts building search-ms federated search connectors for SharePoint
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Extract the remote host from the search-ms crumb and confirm whether the target extension filter is .scr/.exe; check browser history for gobf[.]mx or other CURP-lookalike domains immediately prior. Step 2 (contain): Block the WebDAV host and typosquat domain; quarantine any .scr downloaded from the share. Step 3 (hunt): Look for subsequent .scr execution, Inno Setup child processes, and injection into signed Qihoo 360 (360*.exe) processes on the same host.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessCommandLine has "search-ms:"
| where ProcessCommandLine has_any ("DavWWWRoot", "@SSL@", "crumb")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, InitiatingProcessFileName, FileName, ProcessCommandLine
| order by Timestamp desc
SecurityEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where EventID == 4688
| where CommandLine has "search-ms:"
| where CommandLine has_any ("DavWWWRoot", "@SSL@", "crumb")
| project TimeGenerated, Computer, SubjectUserName, ParentProcessName, NewProcessName, CommandLine
| order by TimeGenerated desc
title: search-ms Protocol Handler Opening Remote WebDAV Share

RTLO / double-extension executable masquerading as a CURP PDF report AIDelivery High
Hunts the most-delivered lure: a .scr executable whose filename was flipped with a right-to-left override (U+202E) to read as a PDF, or padded with a double extension. Detection keys on RTLO characters and pdf/doc/jpg-to-scr/exe double extensions in file writes, the article's specific masquerading trick. Rationale: The article names the lure precisely: a .scr Inno Setup installer whose filename was RTLO-flipped to read as a PDF; U+202E plus doc-to-scr double extensions are near-zero-FP masquerading signals and match a single CURP lure that drove 97.7% of launch events.
ATT&CKT1036.002 T1036.007
Data sourcesEndpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Rare legitimate localized filenames that contain bidirectional text control characters (Arabic/Hebrew document names)
  • Security tooling deliberately writing EICAR-style test files with double extensions
  • Archive extractors preserving mojibake filenames from foreign-language ZIPs
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Render the raw filename bytes to confirm a U+202E override or double extension, then hash the file and check against the six published payload SHA256s. Step 2 (contain): Quarantine the file, isolate the host if executed, and block the delivery WebDAV host. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot on the writing process for search-ms delivery and look for the Inno Setup loader executing and hollowing into a signed Qihoo 360 process.
DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where FileName matches regex @"\x{202E}" or FileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|jpe?g|png)\s*\.(scr|exe)$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, InitiatingProcessAccountName, FileName, FolderPath, InitiatingProcessFileName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImFileEvent
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where TargetFileName matches regex @"\x{202E}" or TargetFileName matches regex @"(?i)\.(pdf|docx?|jpe?g|png)\s*\.(scr|exe)$"
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, TargetFileName, TargetFilePath, ActingProcessName, TargetFileSHA256
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Signed Ubisoft-branded binary executing from a user-writable path (DlrtyGames DLL side-load) AIInstallation Medium
Hunts the DlrtyGames campaign chain where a trojanized DLL is side-loaded through a signed Ubisoft binary to drop a modular .NET RAT. Detection keys on a process whose version-info company is Ubisoft running from a user-writable directory (AppData/Downloads/Temp/ProgramData/Public), the placement pattern required for DLL side-loading. Rationale: The article names a signed Ubisoft binary side-loading a trojanized DLL to drop a .NET RAT in the DlrtyGames directory; anchoring on the Ubisoft signer company plus user-writable execution path captures the staging step. Datadog/Falcon left empty because signer-company (VersionInfo) fields are Defender/ASIM-native and not carried on stock Sysmon/FDR process telemetry.
ATT&CKT1574.002 T1036.005
Data sourcesEndpoint.Processes
Expected false positives · estimated rate: medium — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Ubisoft Connect / Uplay legitimate updater and game launchers that self-update into AppData
  • Portable Ubisoft game copies run from a user Downloads or Desktop folder
  • QA/dev machines running unpackaged Ubisoft builds from Temp
Suppression filter
| where not (InitiatingProcessParentFileName in~ ("UbisoftConnect.exe", "UplayInstaller.exe", "upc.exe"))
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Enumerate DLLs loaded by the Ubisoft binary and flag any DLL from the same user-writable folder (side-load target) or unsigned/mismatched-company DLLs; hash both binary and DLL against the published IOCs. Step 2 (contain): Isolate the host, kill the process, and block C2 addresses 77.110.127.205 / 23.94.252.228. Step 3 (hunt): Pivot to .NET RAT behavior — outbound to the campaign C2 domains and persistence writes across the fleet.
DeviceProcessEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Ubisoft" or InitiatingProcessVersionInfoCompanyName has "Ubisoft"
| where FolderPath has_any ("AppData", "Downloads", "Temp", "ProgramData", "Public")
| where AccountName !endswith "$"
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, AccountName, FileName, FolderPath, ProcessCommandLine, ProcessVersionInfoCompanyName, SHA256
| order by Timestamp desc
ImProcessCreate
| where TimeGenerated > ago(30d)
| where ActingProcessFileCompany has "Ubisoft"
| where ActingProcessName has_any ("AppData", "Downloads", "Temp", "ProgramData", "Public")
| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname, ActorUsername, ActingProcessName, ActingProcessCommandLine, ParentProcessName, ActingProcessFileCompany
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Known Simba Service WebDAV campaign C2 IPs, domains and payload hashes AICommand & Control Medium
Alerts on Rapid7-published indicators for both campaign chains: connections to the C2 IPs/domains or execution/write of any of the six .NET infostealer/RAT payload hashes. Straight IOC coverage to block first, per the article's guidance. Rationale: Uses the exact Rapid7-published C2 IPs (77.110.127.205, 23.94.252.228), campaign domains (gobf.mx, onedrive.cv, google.services.ug, summerartcamp.net) and six payload SHA256 hashes; these are confirmed indicators the article directs defenders to block first. Cross-checked against: • https://github.com/rapid7/Rapid7-Labs
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1105
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic Endpoint.Filesystem
Expected false positives · estimated rate: low — model-assessed, tune to your environment
  • Threat-intel scanners / sandboxes in your own estate deliberately resolving the C2 domains
  • Security researchers detonating the samples in an isolated VLAN that still ships EDR telemetry
  • Passive DNS or URL-reputation appliances pre-fetching the typosquat domain
Response runbook
Step 1 (triage): Confirm the connecting process and whether the source host is a sandbox/research VM vs a production endpoint; correlate to any preceding search-ms/WebDAV or RTLO .scr activity. Step 2 (contain): Block the IPs and domains at egress and quarantine any host matching a payload hash. Step 3 (hunt): Sweep for the WebDAV hijack, RTLO lures, and Ubisoft side-load UCs on any host that touched the C2, and check for Qihoo 360 process hollowing.
let C2Ips = dynamic(["77.110.127.205", "23.94.252.228"]);
let C2Domains = dynamic(["gobf.mx", "onedrive.cv", "google.services.ug", "summerartcamp.net"]);
let Payloads = dynamic(["04a8018191f2e9e76072d072a933371d9d669a42de2b2a087541cd3a653b0ba7", "e8be17a7fbef48b45f1e958b3ae5ebdfcad58808969982c431a905eefcae5268", "449d1121fa275879af22a20407aa7253ac750ac8fa7ff5691101752600d645df", "a88f5ee748e60f889d046718bfe3ddcf1c5f3cba2001cad587e8953a76bf7aa9", "51a02eccdcae0483c7cbb9796738eee6c2a13b740d30e5417cda09bf418ea93b", "82e67735cf822db8f2f759e742e5bf8c54fdbd01a4170619b9e0916e1b3f5923"]);
union
(DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where RemoteIP in (C2Ips) or RemoteUrl has_any (C2Domains)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator = strcat(RemoteIP, " ", RemoteUrl), Proc = InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail = InitiatingProcessCommandLine),
(DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(30d)
| where SHA256 in (Payloads)
| project Timestamp, DeviceName, Account = InitiatingProcessAccountName, Indicator = SHA256, Proc = InitiatingProcessFileName, Detail = FolderPath)
| order by Timestamp desc
let C2Ips = dynamic(["77.110.127.205", "23.94.252.228"]);

union

(ImDnsActivity

| project TimeGenerated, DvcHostname = SrcHostname, SrcIpAddr, Indicator = DnsQuery)
| order by TimeGenerated desc

Beaconing — periodic outbound to small set of destinations Command & Control Medium
C2 channel detection via inter-beacon-time stddev / fan-out to single dest.
ATT&CKT1071.001 T1071.004
Data sourcesNetwork_Traffic.All_Traffic DeviceNetworkEvents
DeviceNetworkEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where RemoteIPType == "Public" and ActionType == "ConnectionSuccess"
| project DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort, Timestamp
| sort by DeviceName asc, RemoteIP asc, RemotePort asc, Timestamp asc
| extend prev_dev = prev(DeviceName, 1), prev_ip = prev(RemoteIP, 1),
         prev_port = prev(RemotePort, 1), prev_ts = prev(Timestamp, 1)
| where DeviceName == prev_dev and RemoteIP == prev_ip and RemotePort == prev_port
| extend delta_sec = datetime_diff('second', Timestamp, prev_ts)
| summarize conn_count = count(), avg_delta = avg(delta_sec), stdev_delta = stdev(delta_sec)
    by DeviceName, RemoteIP, RemotePort
| where conn_count > 30 and avg_delta between (30.0 .. 600.0) and stdev_delta < 5.0
| order by conn_count desc
ImNetworkSession
| where TimeGenerated > ago(2h)
| where DvcAction != "Block"
| where ipv4_is_private(DstIpAddr) == false
| summarize ConnCount = count(),
            DistinctMinutes = dcount(bin(TimeGenerated, 1m))
            by DvcHostname, DstIpAddr, DstPortNumber
| where ConnCount > 50 and DistinctMinutes > 30   // sustained, not bursty
| order by ConnCount desc
NETWORK
Toggle if your env has no CIM data-model acceleration.
| tstats `summariesonly` count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic
    where All_Traffic.action="allowed" AND All_Traffic.dest_category!="internal"
    by _time span=10s, All_Traffic.src, All_Traffic.dest
| `drop_dm_object_name(All_Traffic)`
| streamstats current=f last(_time) AS prev_time by src, dest
| eval delta = _time - prev_time
| stats avg(delta) AS avg_delta stdev(delta) AS sd_delta count by src, dest
| where count > 30 AND sd_delta < 5 AND avg_delta>=30 AND avg_delta<=600
| sort - count
| tstats summariesonly=false count, values(All_Traffic.dest_port) AS ports
    from datamodel=Network_Traffic.All_Traffic

DeviceFileEvents
| where Timestamp > ago(7d)
| where InitiatingProcessAccountName !endswith "$"

| where FileName in~ ("Login Data","Cookies","logins.json","cookies.sqlite")
| where InitiatingProcessFileName !in~ ("chrome.exe","msedge.exe","firefox.exe","brave.exe","opera.exe")

id: 7c8b2e10-4d4f-4a8c-9c1f-bf6e2c4a8d01
status: experimental
description: |

    SQLite databases from Chrome/Edge/Firefox profile directories. Any
    non-browser process touching these files is a high-fidelity signal.
references:

author: Clankerusecase

Data sourcesVulnerabilities DeviceInfo DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
// TVM tables are daily snapshots — pin a 1-day window so the engine
// partitions on Timestamp instead of scanning the full retention.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where Timestamp > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-33053", "CVE-2026-21513", "CVE-2025-24054")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where Timestamp > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId, VulnerabilitySeverityLevel, RecommendedSecurityUpdate
| order by VulnerabilitySeverityLevel asc, DeviceName asc

// Sentinel has no native TVM table. If MDE→Sentinel streaming is enabled,
// `DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities` is available. Otherwise this UC has
// no Sentinel translation — track via Update / Heartbeat OS-version
// gaps as a coarse approximation.
DeviceTvmSoftwareVulnerabilities
| where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)
| where CveId in~ ("CVE-2025-33053", "CVE-2026-21513", "CVE-2025-24054")
| join kind=inner (DeviceInfo | where TimeGenerated > ago(1d)) on DeviceId
| project DeviceName, OSPlatform, CveId,
